title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
Problem III (E410, §§XXVIII–XXIX) asks for the shape of a uniform, weightless elastic wire bent only by forces applied at its ends A and B, i.e. the elastica.

Euler's balance equations for an element are:
- I: dT + V dΦ = 0
- II: dV − T dΦ = 0
- III: d(Vv) = V ds, with bending moment Vv = A dΦ/ds.

Here T is the tangential force (tension), V the normal (shear) force, Φ the tangent angle, s the arclength and A the bending stiffness. The distributed loads vanish: p = q = 0.

§XXVIII, first route. Take ds constant. From III, V = A Φ''. Then:
- From I, dT = −A Φ' Φ'' ds. This integrates to T = B − A Φ'²/2.
- From II, T = V'/Φ' = A Φ'''/Φ'.
- Eliminating T gives 2A Φ'''/Φ' + A Φ'² = 2B.
- Multiplying by 4Φ'Φ''/A and integrating gives 4Φ''² + Φ'⁴ = (4B/A)Φ'² + C.

Put u = Φ' (the curvature κ). The result is the intrinsic first integral of the elastica in terms of curvature, (du/ds)² = C/4 + (B/A)u² − u⁴/4. Equivalently, u'' + u³/2 − (B/A)u = 0, the now-standard curvature equation of Euler elastica. It integrates by the elliptic quadrature s = ∫ 2du/√(C + (4B/A)u² − u⁴). Euler drops this route as 'nimis molestus'.

§XXIX, second route. From I and II, T dT + V dV = 0, so T² + V² = C², a constant end-force resultant. Then dΦ = dV/√(C² − V²), giving V = C sin(Φ + D) and T = C cos(Φ + D). Choosing the reference direction sets D = 0. On the next page this gives A Φ'' = C sin Φ, the pendulum-type equation. Its first integral is A Φ'² = B − 2C cos Φ, which gives the curvature radius and the coordinates.

A quick check links the two routes. Using route one, T² + V² = (B − Au²/2)² + A²u'² = B² + A²C/4. So the first route's constants encode the resultant: C_res² = B² + A²C/4. Euler does not remark on this.
errors: The final quadrature has a dropped factor 2. From du = ds·√(C/4 + (B/A)u² − u⁴/4) = (ds/2)·√(C + (4B/A)u² − u⁴), it follows that ds = 2du/√(C + (4B/A)u² − u⁴), not du/√(...). This is harmless because Euler abandons the route.
The constants B and C of §XXVIII are not the same as the B and C of §XXIX/XXX (C becomes the resultant force there). The reuse of letters is confusing but not an error.

ideas.what: Equilibrium of a rod element in tangential/normal components: dT + V dΦ = 0, dV − T dΦ = 0, d(moment) = V ds, with moment = A·curvature
ideas.modern_name: Intrinsic (Frenet-frame) equilibrium equations of a planar Kirchhoff/Euler–Bernoulli rod
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E410, 1771), as emphasized by Truesdell; later Kirchhoff (1859)
ideas.where_published: E410 Novi Comm. 15 (1771); discussed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II.11/2)

ideas.what: Curvature of the elastica as a function of arclength satisfies κ'' + κ³/2 − λκ = 0, with first integral κ'² = C/4 + λκ² − κ⁴/4, so κ is an elliptic function of s
ideas.modern_name: Intrinsic curvature equation of Euler elastica (as used by Langer–Singer, Mumford, Bryant–Griffiths)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Often presented as a modern variational derivation (e.g. Langer & Singer 1984; Mumford 1994), with roots in Euler
ideas.where_published: Here, E410 §XXVIII (1771); whether Truesdell's commentary highlights this specific curvature ODE: unsure

ideas.what: T² + V² = const, so the internal force has constant magnitude and V = C sin Φ, T = C cos Φ
ideas.modern_name: Constancy of the internal force resultant (conservation of force in an unloaded rod)

ideas.what: Reduction to A Φ'' = C sin Φ (next page), the same equation as the pendulum
ideas.where_published: E410 §XXX; the equation also appears in the 1744 Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum I in other variables; the analogy itself is not stated by Euler

missed.claim: Euler derives the intrinsic curvature equation of the elastica and its elliptic quadrature in κ, then abandons it as too laborious. This curvature-based route is exactly the one taken in modern geometric treatments (Langer–Singer, Mumford's elastica in computer vision). Euler's priority for this explicit form of the curvature ODE in 1771 is rarely cited in that literature.
missed.quote: 4ddΦ² + dΦ⁴ = 4B/A · ds² · dΦ² + C ds⁴ ... Verum hoc modo calculus fit nimis molestus
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is historical credit for the κ-equation of free elastica, which underlies elastic-curve and Willmore-type literature. It shows Euler had the 'curvature is an elliptic function of arclength' viewpoint.

missed.claim: The two routes Euler gives are linked by the identity (resultant force)² = B² + A²C/4. This ties the first integral of the curvature equation to the conserved force magnitude, an instance of conservation from translational symmetry (Noether-type). Euler does not make this link explicit.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Minor. It is well known in modern elastica theory that the integration constants correspond to conserved force and moment, so this is mostly pedagogical.

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains an explicit 1771 derivation of the modern intrinsic curvature ODE of the elastica and its elliptic quadrature (with a factor-2 slip). E410 is well studied by Truesdell, so it is probably known to historians, but modern geometric papers usually do not credit Euler for this form.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image; the final formula is printed as ds = du/√(C + 4B/A·uu − u⁴), and the missing factor 2 is Euler's own slip, not a transcription error.
In the header-supplied title, 'flesibilium' should read 'flexibilium'.
